source.version: Corrected journal version of record: published 30 September 2025, corrected 09 February 2026 (p. 1). Complete local article and markdown read; separate online supplementary material not read.
source.title_on_document: Exploring creativity in human–AI co-creation: a comparative study across design experience

supplement.holds: The main article refers to semi-structured interview material (p. 4, Section 3.1), analysis results for paired and independent-samples t-tests and ANOVA (pp. 8 and 10, Sections 4.1–4.3), and representative low- and high-rated design outputs in Supplementary Figures 1 and 2 (p. 8, Section 4). These separate materials are not included in this PDF and were not read.

paper_design_summary: Preliminary interviews with 13 professional designers informed a human–AI co-creative design process (p. 4, Section 3.1). In the main online comparison, 42 designers, comprising 21 novices and 21 experienced designers, all completed a traditional character-design task first and the AI-assisted task second, with no randomized order (pp. 6–8, Sections 3.2.1–3.2.4 and Table 2). Blinded experts scored novelty, quality, and refinement of the submitted designs; submitted concepts were counted, and perceived creative support was self-reported (pp. 7–8, Sections 3.2.3–3.2.4).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Every participant followed the same fixed sequence: Traditional Creative Design Process (TCDP), then Human–AI Co-Creative Design Process (HAI-CDP). Design process varied within people; novice versus experienced status was a pre-existing between-person characteristic.
assignment.quote: All participants first completed the TCDP phase and then proceeded to the HAI-CDP phase.
assignment.locator: p. 7, Section 3.2.4, Experimental procedure and data collection; p. 8, Table 2 (TCDP round followed by HAI-CDP round); pp. 6–7, Section 3.2.2 (experience groups).

arms.name: Traditional Creative Design Process (TCDP)
arms.description: First condition for all 42 designers (21 novices and 21 experienced). Google Search and Pinterest for references and inspiration; Adobe Photoshop and Procreate for illustration and refinement. These are the same people as in the HAI-CDP condition (pp. 6–8, Sections 3.2.2 and 3.2.4; Table 2).

arms.name: Human–AI Co-Creative Design Process (HAI-CDP)
arms.description: Second condition for the same 42 designers (21 novices and 21 experienced). ChatGPT supported concept definition; Midjourney and Stable Diffusion supported visual exploration and iterative development. Counts overlap completely with TCDP (pp. 6–8, Sections 3.2.2 and 3.2.4; Table 2).

participants.who: 21 second-year undergraduate animation or visual-design students with no real-world design-project experience, and 21 experienced designers with more than 3 years of work in animation or visual design. The same people completed both process conditions; the arm counts must not be added.
participants.quote: A total of 42 designers participated in the experiment, including 21 novices and 21 experienced designers.
participants.locator: pp. 6–7, Section 3.2.2 (sample and experience groups); p. 7, Section 3.2.4 (everyone completed both conditions); p. 8, Section 4 (analysis groups: n = 21 per experience group).

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT; Midjourney; Stable Diffusion. Model versions not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: ChatGPT generated conceptual descriptions, design inspiration, and reference materials during concept definition. Midjourney and Stable Diffusion generated visual concepts from text prompts during visual exploration and design development, followed by iterative refinement (p. 7, Section 3.2.4).

task.description: Online character concept design on the theme “Mechanical Beings of a Future World”: produce a range of visual concepts and a written rationale describing inspiration, defining features, and the core conceptual narrative (p. 6, Section 3.2.1).
task.duration: 48 h for each design-process condition (p. 8, Table 2).

contrasts.reported: HAI-CDP versus TCDP: the reported two-way ANOVA main effect of design process was F(1, 80) = 448, p < 0.001, with higher novelty under HAI-CDP. For novice designers, HAI-CDP M = 3.43, SD = 0.40 versus TCDP M = 1.87, SD = 0.31. Ratings used a 5-point scale and were averaged across three blinded experts.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 4.3 (design-process main effect); p. 9, Section 4.2 (novice means and SDs); pp. 7–8, Sections 3.2.3–3.2.4 (measure and scoring); p. 8, Section 4 (participant groups).

contrasts.reported: HAI-CDP versus TCDP: the reported two-way ANOVA main effect of design process was F(1, 80) = 377, p < 0.001, with higher quality under HAI-CDP. For experienced designers, HAI-CDP M = 4.36, SD = 0.26 versus TCDP M = 2.49, SD = 0.36. Reported paired t-tests: novice designers t = 13.974, p < 0.001; experienced designers t = 21.359, p < 0.001. Quality assessed narrative/style alignment and completeness of details, using a 5-point scale averaged across three blinded experts.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 4.3 (design-process main effect); p. 9, Section 4.2 (experienced means and SDs); p. 8, Section 4.1 (paired tests); pp. 7–8, Sections 3.2.3–3.2.4 (measure and scoring).

outcomes.name: Number of ideas generated (submitted character-design concepts)
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: HAI-CDP versus TCDP: the reported two-way ANOVA main effect of design process was F(1, 80) = 178, p < 0.001, with more ideas under HAI-CDP. For experienced designers, HAI-CDP M = 4.76, SD = 0.89 versus TCDP M = 2.38, SD = 0.50. Reported paired t-tests: novice designers t = 8.919, p < 0.001; experienced designers t = 12.619, p < 0.001. Idea count was the total number of design outcomes each participant ultimately submitted.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 4.3 (design-process main effect); p. 9, Section 4.2 (experienced means and SDs); p. 8, Section 4.1 (paired tests); p. 7, Section 3.2.4 (count definition).

outcomes.name: Level of refinement of character designs (expert ratings)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Richness and precision of visual details in the submitted character designs. Three experts independently rated each design under a blind review procedure using a 5-point Likert scale; the final refinement score was the arithmetic mean of their ratings (p. 7, Sections 3.2.2–3.2.4; p. 8, Section 3.2.4 continuation).

contrasts.reported: HAI-CDP versus TCDP: the reported two-way ANOVA main effect of design process was F(1, 80) = 619, p < 0.001, with higher refinement under HAI-CDP. For experienced designers, HAI-CDP M = 4.17, SD = 0.27 versus TCDP M = 2.55, SD = 0.30. Reported paired t-tests: novice designers t = 19.481, p < 0.001; experienced designers t = 21.855, p < 0.001. The results report n = 21 per experience group; the same participants completed both conditions.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 4.3 (design-process main effect); p. 9, Section 4.2 (experienced means and SDs); p. 8, Section 4.1 (paired tests) and Section 4 (group counts); pp. 7–8, Sections 3.2.3–3.2.4 (measure, scoring, and fixed sequence).

studies.label: Preliminary designer interviews for model construction (first stage)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Not applicable to an intervention contrast: the preliminary dataset consists of qualitative interviews about existing design practices. No allocation to assistance conditions is described.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1, Construction of the Human–AI Co-Creative Design Process model.

participants.who: Professional visual-design and animation designers with over 3 years of practical project experience; their interview transcripts were coded to develop the design-process model.
participants.quote: This study conducted semi-structured interviews with 13 professional designers from the fields of visual design and animation. All participants had over 3 years of practical project experience.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1 (sample and coding of interview data); p. 5, Table 1 (coding analysis).

ai_tool.name_model: Tools reported in design practice included ChatGPT, Claude AI, Gemini, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, DALL·E, and Canva AI; no assigned model or version.
ai_tool.how_used: Interviewees described how they used AI tools in existing creative projects and at different design stages; this was qualitative model-development evidence, not an assigned creative-task comparison (p. 4, Section 3.1).

task.description: Semi-structured interviews about AI-assisted design experience and the design stages in which AI was integrated; transcripts underwent hierarchical qualitative coding. No creative-output score was reported for this dataset (pp. 4–5, Section 3.1 and Table 1).
task.duration: The text states: “Each interview lasted between 15 min.” (p. 4, Section 3.1).

eligibility.reason: The main comparison explicitly imposed TCDP first and HAI-CDP second for everyone; neither assistance nor condition order was randomized (p. 7, Section 3.2.4; p. 8, Table 2). Only 42 people were analyzed, with 21 in each experience group, and both conditions used the same participants (p. 6, Section 3.2.2; p. 8, Section 4). Expert ratings of submitted designs and counts of submitted concepts meet the output-scoring criterion (pp. 7–8, Sections 3.2.3–3.2.4). This fixed-sequence comparison is observational context under the codebook. The preliminary interviews with 13 designers are model-development evidence without scored creative outputs and cannot be added to the task sample to satisfy the sample-size criterion (p. 4, Section 3.1).

one_line_finding: In the fixed-sequence comparison of 42 designers, the AI-assisted phase had higher novelty, quality, and idea count than the preceding traditional phase (reported process main effects: F(1, 80) = 448, 377, and 178, respectively; all p < 0.001), but order was not randomized (p. 10, Section 4.3; pp. 6–7, Sections 3.2.2 and 3.2.4).

applied.quote: Design refinement measures the richness and precision of the visual details presented.
